**The meaning of the hadith**
Anger is an instinct that Allah has placed in human nature. It is a change that happens when the blood of the heart boils up, so that the chest may find relief through it. People differ in how it starts and what it leads to, and so some of it is praiseworthy and some of it blameworthy. Whoever's anger is for the truth, and does not drag him into what ruins his religion and his worldly life, that is praiseworthy anger. And whoever gets angry for falsehood, or cannot control his anger when he is angry, so that anger drags him to overstep the limits and ruin his religion and his worldly life, that is blameworthy anger.

In this hadith Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, relates that a man — named Jariyah ibn Qudamah, may Allah be pleased with him — asked the Prophet ﷺ for advice, and he ﷺ advised him not to get angry, and this is understood to mean blameworthy anger. … It has been said that it means: avoid the causes of anger and do not expose yourself to what brings it on; as for anger itself, it cannot be forbidden, because it is something natural that does not leave one's nature. … And it has been said that it means: do not do what your anger commands you to do. In his saying "Do not get angry" he ﷺ gathered the good of this world and the Hereafter, because anger leads to cutting ties and to holding back gentleness, and it may lead to harming the one you are angry with.

📖 From the Hadith Encyclopedia — Dorar.net.

**Talk with your child**
1. When the bucket tipped over from Thamir's hand, how many seedlings did Thamir ruin? And how many did Badr ruin after that in his anger? And who had more reason to apologise?
2. What did Badr do when the goat bit the seedling? And what did he remember, so that he sat down and kept quiet?
3. Badr used to say, "That's just how I was made." Is anger itself a sin? (No, it is a feeling everyone has. What is blameworthy is doing what it tells us to do: shouting, breaking things and hurting others. The way to deal with it is to sit down and keep quiet until it goes away, as Badr did.)

**This week's exercise**
Agree on "Badr's plan" and write it on a sheet of paper on the fridge door: When I get angry, I sit down, keep quiet, and count to ten in my head before I speak. At the end of each day, your child tells you about a time they tried the plan, even if it did not work every time.
